analysis.investment_thesis: Neogen has built an impressive 9-year revenue CAGR of 25.6% across bromine, lithium, and Grignard chemistries with genuine exposure to the battery materials megatrend — but the company is currently in a debt-fueled overexpansion that has driven net profits from ₹50 Cr to ₹35 Cr over two years while FCF has been negative every single year. At 150x trailing P/E with ROE of only 5.6%, the market is paying a premium growth price for a business currently delivering sub-par returns on capital.
key_strengths: 9-year revenue CAGR of 25.6% and EBITDA CAGR of 27.2% demonstrate a genuinely compounding specialty chemicals franchise
Diversified chemistry platform (bromine, lithium, Grignard) serves pharma, agrochem, and emerging battery materials — the lithium/EV pivot addresses a multi-decade TAM
51.2% promoter holding with exports to 33 countries signals management conviction and global market acceptance
key_risks: Net profit is declining — ₹50 Cr (FY23) → ₹36 Cr (FY24) → ₹35 Cr (FY25) — as finance costs (₹48 Cr) nearly match earnings; debt has surged from ₹137 Cr to ₹1,132 Cr in five years (D/E 1.41)
FCF has been negative every year in the dataset; ₹318 Cr capex in FY25 and ₹335 Cr CWIP signal a capacity bet whose returns are unproven
ROE of 5.6% and ROCE of 8.8% are far below Fisher's 20%+ threshold — the business is not yet generating returns commensurate with its equity base or current valuation
red_flags: Finance costs of ₹48 Cr in FY25 nearly eclipse net profit of ₹35 Cr — a classic sign of over-leverage squeezing equity holders
Other Income turned sharply negative at -₹10 Cr in FY25 (from +₹8 Cr in FY24) — unusual and unexplained swing demands investigation
Cash on hand collapsed to ₹5 Cr against ₹1,132 Cr in borrowings — liquidity buffer is dangerously thin if capex cycle extends
Borrowings line (₹1,132 Cr) is substantially higher than Total Debt (₹597 Cr) as reported — data inconsistency warrants scrutiny of off-balance-sheet obligations
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Neogen's historical growth record is genuinely impressive by Fisher standards — 25.6% revenue CAGR and 27.2% EBITDA CAGR over nine years reflect a real competitive position in niche organobromine and organolithium chemistry. The company's pivot toward battery-grade lithium salts and Grignard reagents for EV supply chains is exactly the kind of new-product market extension Fisher admired. Management is clearly investing heavily for future capacity, as evidenced by ₹335 Cr of CWIP and ₹318 Cr of capex in FY25 alone. The scuttlebutt case would be that Neogen is building the equivalent of an IP moat in specialty lithium chemistry before larger players enter.

However, the current financials fail Fisher's fundamental test: a great business must earn high returns on invested capital. ROE of 5.6% and ROCE of 8.8% are not great-company metrics — they are the metrics of a commodity cyclical burdened by debt. Finance costs have grown at a 28.6% CAGR identical to revenue growth, meaning every rupee of growth is being offset by a rupee of interest expense. Net profits have now declined two consecutive years despite rising revenues. FCF has been negative in all five years shown, and cash is essentially zero. At 150x trailing P/E, the market is pricing in a sharp and near-certain earnings recovery from the new capacity; if the ramp-up is delayed by even one or two years, downside is severe. I would wait for evidence of FCF inflection and ROE recovery above 15% before revisiting.
